claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the trip ran 24.7 km against an optimal 21.6 km, i.e. 3.2 km (+15%) more than the shortest most direct route.

A single off-route segment from 09:32 to 09:38 added 2.96 km while the optimal route covered 0.00 km on that stretch, and the vehicle reached 974 m away from the optimal route; this segment is an un-exempted deviation under RD-1.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total $53.17 with distance $34.84 at 24.7 km and time $12.96 at 49.8 min), so the extra detour kilometres flow directly into the metered fare and are refundable at the per-km rate.

The metre billed exactly the 3.2 km excess distance at $1.41/km, i.e. $4.45, which is the excess-distance component of the fare to be refunded against the un-exempted segment's 2.96 km at the trip's per-km rate ($1.41 = $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km).

No in-app chat exists between rider and driver, so there was no passenger request for a stop or route change and no passenger agreement to the deviation; the driver's assertion that he 'followed my GPS' cannot override the GPS record.

The driver's congestion excuse is unsupported: no traffic incident was recorded near the route in the trip window, and the only speed-band records (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard, band 4 = 30–39 km/h) are not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires, nor do they attach to the substituted portion of the optimal route.

The trip took 49.8 min against a 28 min estimate (+21.4 min), consistent with an unexplained 09:32–09:38 detour rather than normal traffic; weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, excluding weather as a cause.
The driver has 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days (of 2 filed), so this upheld route deviation makes the conduct repeated and warrants an account-review flag alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The GPS excess (3.2 km per F1) is larger than the single off-route segment's added distance (2.96 km per F3); under RD-2 only the un-exempted segment is refundable, so the driver will argue the ~0.24 km residual is map-matching noise rather than chargeable detour, capping the refund below the full $4.45.

The 49.8 min duration against a 28 min estimate (F2) and the band 4 speeds on East Coast Parkway / Airport Boulevard (F9, F10) give the driver an opening to argue ordinary congestion made a reroute reasonable under RD-4, even though no qualifying incident exists (F11) and band 4 is not band 1–2.

The driver's statement (F8) is the only account of why he diverted; there is no chat denial from the rider (F7 is empty), so the judge must rest entirely on GPS and traffic records to reject his 'GPS rerouted me' explanation.
The rider profile shows 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver may use to paint the rider as a repeat complainant, though profile facts cannot decide the case.

No traffic incident (accident / roadwork / breakdown / road block / heavy traffic) is recorded near the route in the trip window, so the diversion segment cannot be exempted under the RD-4 incident limb; the driver's exposure is limited to the segment's extra kilometres only, not to waiting or other charges (waiting $0.00 in F6).

The client's own statement (F8, 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') is not a defence the policy accepts: RD-4 requires traffic-incident evidence, and F9/F10 are only band-4 (30–39 km/h) records, which under RD-4(b) are corroborative at best and cannot exempt a segment on their own.

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the trip ran 24.7 km against an optimal 21.6 km, i.e. 3.2 km (+15%) more than the shortest most direct route.

A single off-route segment from 09:32 to 09:38 added 2.96 km while the optimal route covered 0.00 km on that stretch, and the vehicle reached 974 m away from the optimal route; this segment is an un-exempted deviation under RD-1.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total $53.17 with distance $34.84 at 24.7 km and time $12.96 at 49.8 min), so the extra detour kilometres flow directly into the metered fare and are refundable at the per-km rate.

The metre billed exactly the 3.2 km excess distance at $1.41/km, i.e. $4.45, which is the excess-distance component of the fare to be refunded against the un-exempted segment's 2.96 km at the trip's per-km rate ($1.41 = $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km).

No in-app chat exists between rider and driver, so there was no passenger request for a stop or route change and no passenger agreement to the deviation; the driver's assertion that he 'followed my GPS' cannot override the GPS record.

The driver's congestion excuse is unsupported: no traffic incident was recorded near the route in the trip window, and the only speed-band records (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard, band 4 = 30–39 km/h) are not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires, nor do they attach to the substituted portion of the optimal route.

The trip took 49.8 min against a 28 min estimate (+21.4 min), consistent with an unexplained 09:32–09:38 detour rather than normal traffic; weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, excluding weather as a cause.
The driver has 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days (of 2 filed), so this upheld route deviation makes the conduct repeated and warrants an account-review flag alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The GPS excess (3.2 km per F1) is larger than the single off-route segment's added distance (2.96 km per F3); under RD-2 only the un-exempted segment is refundable, so the driver will argue the ~0.24 km residual is map-matching noise rather than chargeable detour, capping the refund below the full $4.45.

The 49.8 min duration against a 28 min estimate (F2) and the band 4 speeds on East Coast Parkway / Airport Boulevard (F9, F10) give the driver an opening to argue ordinary congestion made a reroute reasonable under RD-4, even though no qualifying incident exists (F11) and band 4 is not band 1–2.

The driver's statement (F8) is the only account of why he diverted; there is no chat denial from the rider (F7 is empty), so the judge must rest entirely on GPS and traffic records to reject his 'GPS rerouted me' explanation.
The rider profile shows 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver may use to paint the rider as a repeat complainant, though profile facts cannot decide the case.

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered service: the $53.17 charged breaks down into base $3.90 + distance $34.84 (24.7 km) + time $12.96 (49.8 min) + platform $1.47, i.e. it follows the meter and contains no unpublished add-on, so no post-trip surcharge item is recoverable under FARE-1.

Only one off-route segment is recorded (F3, 09:32–09:38, 2.96 km, max 974 m from optimal), and there is no second or third such segment, so the refund exposure is capped at that single segment and no further deviation can be argued from the +3.2 km total in F1.

The driver's statement that he followed his GPS (F8) is consistent with the recorded off-route segment being a single continuous 2.96 km diversion inside a 49.8-minute trip rather than repeated wandering, and no chat record exists in which the rider requested any route change (F7).

Congestion on the corridor during the trip is documented (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard both at speed band 4, 30–39 km/h, 08:58–10:01) and the weather was fair, so the trip-time blowout (49.8 min vs 28 min estimated, F2) is not attributable to driver conduct alone.

No traffic incident (accident / roadwork / breakdown / road block / heavy traffic) is recorded near the route in the trip window, so the diversion segment cannot be exempted under the RD-4 incident limb; the driver's exposure is limited to the segment's extra kilometres only, not to waiting or other charges (waiting $0.00 in F6).
The driver's account shows a 1.1-year history with a 4.8 rating over 968 trips in 90 days and one previously upheld dispute, so RD-6's repeated-offender account flag is not made out on this record.

Any mileage-only recovery is bounded by the fare facts: the segment added 2.96 km and the trip per-km rate is $1.41 (distance fare $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km), giving a maximum of about $4.17 for the single unexcused segment, and the $4.45 'excess distance billed' figure in F4 is a whole-trip excess that cannot be awarded on top.

weaknesses: The core finding goes against the client: F3 records an unexcused off-route segment of 2.96 km that the optimal route covers in 0.00 km, and with F11 showing no traffic incident near the route, RD-4 offers no exemption — so the rider will win a mileage refund of roughly $4.17 on F3 + F6.

The client's own statement (F8, 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') is not a defence the policy accepts: RD-4 requires traffic-incident evidence, and F9/F10 are only band-4 (30–39 km/h) records, which under RD-4(b) are corroborative at best and cannot exempt a segment on their own.

F1 (+3.2 km, +15%) and F2 (49.8 vs 28 min) will be used by the rider to argue the detour was more than a trivial episode; RD-1 sets no percentage or kilometre threshold, so the small size of the segment does not by itself defeat the claim.
The absence of any chat (F7) removes the RD-5 route-agreement defence entirely; if the rider argues the driver chose the stopping route alone, RD-3(b) also works against the client.

points.response: Conceded on scope: I do not seek any unpublished surcharge. Waiting was $0.00 and the only recoverable amount is the detour mileage, which under RD-2 for a RydeTAXI trip is Σ(extra_km) × per-km rate, computed from F4 and F6.

Accepting a single segment does not shrink the exposure: F3 records 2.96 km of off-route mileage where the optimal route covers 0.00 km, and RD-1 has no kilometre or percentage threshold, so that one un-exempted segment alone supports the refund — my C2 and C4 rest on F3, not on the residual in F1.

The driver's 'my GPS rerouted me' statement (F8) is a user statement and loses to the system GPS record where they conflict: F3 shows the vehicle up to 974 m off the optimal route for six minutes, and F8 offers no traffic-incident evidence, which is what RD-4 requires.

Band 4 (30–39 km/h) is not 'severe congestion': RD-4(b) contemplates band 1–2 (0 < 9, 10 < 19 km/h) and, per RD-4, band evidence alone cannot exempt a segment, so F9 and F10 corroborate nothing here; the fair weather in F12 removes weather as an alternative cause.

The driver's own concession that no incident is recorded (F11) and that no exemption applies is precisely my case: F3 stands as an un-exempted segment, and RD-2 then fixes the refund as that segment's extra kilometres times the trip's per-km rate.

I do not press RD-6 as a standalone finding: the flag is only an add-on under RD-6 and profile facts (F14) cannot decide anything, so I am content for the account-review flag to rest on the upheld deviation itself rather than on the history.

This matches my own arithmetic and I do not ask for more: F3's 2.96 km at the per-km rate derived from F6 ($34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km) gives $4.17, and F4's $4.45 whole-trip excess is not claimed on top of it.

Conceded as to the numbers, but the claim proves too much: RD-2 refunds only the un-exempted segment's extra kilometres, and F3 fixes that at 2.96 km, so the 0.24 km gap between F1's +3.2 km and F3's 2.96 km falls outside the refundable measure.
Not contested: the 09:32–09:38 record in F3 is a single un-exempted off-route segment of 2.96 km under RD-1, and I do not argue a second segment exists anywhere in the GPS record.

The metered character of the trip is right, but RD-2 refunds 'only the mileage unit' — the claimed time component of $12.96 (F6) and the platform fee $1.47 are not detour mileage and cannot be pulled into the refund.

F4's $4.45 is the meter's excess over the whole optimal 21.6 km, not over the un-exempted segment; pricing only that segment at $1.41/km (F6: $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km × 2.96 km) yields about $4.17, and awarding $4.45 would double-count the 0.24 km residual RD-2 excludes as matching residual.
Accepted that F7 shows no chat and F8 cannot override the GPS record; I make no RD-3 or RD-5 defence, since exemption would require evidence in the traffic facts that F11 shows does not exist.
I do not claim RD-4 exemption: F11 shows no incident, and F9/F10 at band 4 (30–39 km/h) are at most corroborative under RD-4(b), so the segment stands as un-exempted and is refunded, not exempted.

The 49.8 min against the 28 min estimate (F2) over a route with fair weather (F12) does not convert the un-exempted segment into a larger refund: RD-2's measure is extra kilometres only, and the 2.96 km segment is already the whole of the chargeable deviation in F3.

RD-6's flag requires the profile's route-dispute count: F14 shows the driver's single upheld dispute was a no-show (route: 0), so this route deviation is not a repeat route violation and no flag_account attaches.
